If I reserve too few, we hire freelancers at the last minute for about three times the price; if I reserve too many, we pay a small fee for each guide we do not use. My director asked me for a machine learning model that forecasts how many bookings we will receive per destination each month. The table I shared is our booking export up to late February 2026: one row per booking with the booking date, travel date, destination, nationality, channel, lead time in days, price, whether it had free cancellation, and whether it was cancelled. I will use the result myself every month to fix the reservation. [shares bookings.csv]

Here's how I see the work, and where I'd start.

**The problem as it really is.** Your monthly decision is how many guides to reserve per destination for the month after next. Your director asked for an ML model that forecasts bookings per destination per month, and you'll use the result yourself to fix the reservation. What's known: your booking export runs to late February 2026 (1,500 rows), with booking and travel dates, destination, nationality, channel, lead time, price, free cancellation flag, and cancellation flag. What's not known yet: whether one booking means one guide is needed, how many bookings actually travel (cancellations), and how far ahead bookings typically arrive (lead time).

**What needs care before any work.** Bookings are not guides — a booking may need more or less than one guide, and group size isn't in the export, so I'm assuming one booking = one guide need; you can correct me. Cancelled bookings must not count as demand. And plain ML that minimizes average error is the wrong target for your cost structure: under-reserving costs about three times the price of a reserved guide, while over-reserving costs a small fee per unused guide. So we shouldn't aim for the most likely number of bookings — we should aim for a reservation level that weighs those two costs (effectively a high quantile of expected demand). I'll also make sure no column written after the reservation decision leaks into the forecast.

**The approach.** Instead of a straight forecast of total bookings, I'd forecast net bookings — bookings not cancelled — per destination per travel month, using only information available when you place the reservation, then convert the forecast into a guide count using your 3:1 cost ratio. 1. Explore the export: date range, destinations, cancellation rate, lead times — checking how much history each destination has. If a destination has too little history for a monthly model, I'll tell you and we pool it or simplify.
2. Build the target: net bookings per destination per travel month, with features from before the reservation cutoff; verify no leakage.
3. Model demand per destination per month, set each reservation at the cost-optimal level, and compare against the baseline.
4. Deliver monthly recommended guide numbers per destination with the reasoning, set up for your monthly refresh.

Steps 1–2 need nothing from you; step 3 runs once you choose an approach; step 4 is what you'd use each month. I'd stop at step 1 if the data is too thin per destination and recommend a simpler destination-level rule instead.

- **Forecast demand, then set reservations by cost** (prediction model): a monthly recommended guide count per destination with the cost reasoning — more up-front work, optimizes your actual decision, assumes one booking = one guide.
- **Describe what actually happened by destination and month** (dashboard): net bookings, cancellations, and lead times refreshed each month so you choose the number yourself — quick and transparent, but you carry the under/over-reserving risk.

transcript.text: I am the head of marketing at a subscription company. The board asked for an AI segmentation of our customers, and I would like five or six segments with names we can put on a slide. The table I shared has one row per customer: signup date, the segment we already record, city, plan, tenure in months, monthly spend, support tickets in the last 90 days, and whether they churned the next month. Next quarter my team can run at most three email campaigns: one to move people to a higher plan, one to keep people who look likely to leave, and one welcome series for new customers. The same person should not receive two of them. My campaign managers will use the segments to decide who gets which campaign. [shares customers.csv]

I understood you to want five or six named customer segments for a board slide, and then to use those same segments to assign each customer to at most one of three email campaigns next quarter: an upsell to a higher plan, a retention save for customers likely to leave, and a welcome series for new customers. No customer should receive two campaigns, and your campaign managers will apply the segments.

I'm assuming the goal is named, slide-ready segments plus a campaign-assignment rule; the decision is which campaign (or none) each of your 1,200 customers receives; and the users are your campaign managers. The table has one row per customer with signup date, current segment, city, plan, tenure, monthly spend, recent support tickets, and a churned-next-month flag — confirmed: 1,200 rows, nine columns.

Before we build, two things need care. First, a slide-ready segmentation is not the same as a campaign assignment: a clustering could put the same customer in both an upsell and a retention group, breaking your one-campaign rule. Second, churned_next_month is known only after the decision to leave, so using it as a feature for every segment can leak the answer and overstate how clean the segments are. I'd build segments around campaign eligibility first — new = welcome, high churn risk = retention, upgrade-ready = upsell, everyone else = no campaign — then split those into five or six named groups for the slide. That beats the obvious "run clustering and name clusters" because it guarantees your one-person-one-campaign rule and gives managers a direct rule, not just a picture.

Two ways to begin:

The first option builds the campaign-oriented segmentation straight away — segments designed for the campaigns, named for the slide, with mutual-exclusion rules so nobody gets two emails. The second profiles the customer base first — current segment mix, churn by plan/tenure/tickets, spend distribution — so the names and rules fit the real data before anything is named.

Two years ago we built a model that scores every new lead on how likely it is to become a customer, and the sales team calls the highest scores first. Since the autumn the sales team says the top leads are much worse than they used to be, and my manager wants me to retrain with a larger model and more features. I have the old training set and every lead since, not yet exported. What would you do?

The decision is really: *how do we fix lead scoring so sales calls leads that actually become paying customers?* The people who act are the sales team (who call the top scores), you (who rebuild), and your manager (who decides the approach).

**What needs care before any work.** Retraining with a bigger model and more features would likely bake in the wrong target. Old labels (first payment) and new labels (trial start) measure different things, so mixing them teaches the model to chase trial signups rather than paying customers. You also cannot simply add features when two existing ones no longer exist, and partner-marketplace leads may convert differently from your own leads. "Leads are worse" is ambiguous too — worse at converting to trial, or worse at paying? Sales and finance now count differently, so the decline may be partly a measurement artifact, not a real drop in lead quality.
